10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing...
  • It has been revealed that way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand.
  • In a recent development, here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

It has been revealed that way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

I couldn’t have been more wrong.

In a recent development, here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

According to recent reports, the man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

Industry observers note that it’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

Recent findings suggest that this one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

Sources indicate that when Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

Recent findings suggest that what makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Recent findings suggest that henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he says: “It's kind of like being a father.”.

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Industry observers note that henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

Sources indicate that but Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

According to recent reports, ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

With a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

Sources indicate that when Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

According to recent reports, here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

In a recent development, after Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He demonstrates Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Sources indicate that physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that says “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”.

It has been revealed that it's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

Industry observers note that during their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”.

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Industry observers note that kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Sources indicate that ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

Sources indicate that but the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He showed his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry indicates the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They look high-effort but we promise they’re not.

Sure, it’d be nice to be the person with the time and energy to make an elaborate chocolate-and-matcha checkerboard loaf cake, or a homemade pavlova piled high with syrupy berries. But in reality, most of us don’t even have time to shower as much as we’d like during the week. So, whether you have a party you need to bring a dish to or you just want a little sweet treat at the end of the day, consider these simple desserts that look impressive but take very few brain cells to actually complete. (We used them all up already, OK?) You won’t even need the oven for most of them.

Cool, creamy layers with a dark chocolate frosting on top? That doesn’t sound bad at all. Princess Pinky Girl’s chocolate eclair cake is an easy icebox cake-style recipe that’ll serve a big group with ease.

Recent findings suggest that this slow-cooker apple-pear crisp from Damn Delicious will make your whole house smell incredible; by the time it’s ready to eat, you’ll be more than ready to plop a scoop of ice cream on top and chow down. The sweet, crispy pecan topping really takes this to the next level.

A Beautiful Plate’s strawberry mascarpone tart is such a beautiful dessert, but surprisingly, the hardest part about making it is just arranging the berry slices on top. And don’t worry, her recipe explains precisely how to lay them out to get that bakery case look.

In a recent development, averie Cooks’ caramel apple nachos are such a cute idea for a movie night with your kids. They’re ridiculously easy to make and customize with your favorite toppings, but they still feel like an extra-special snack.

Family Fresh Meals is kind of a genius for this hack: Make a simple fresh fruit jam and use it to top a scoop of vanilla ice cream to wow your guests, or just treat yourself. Her recipe is incredibly easy and makes a substantial batch of jam you can use for all sorts of dishes.

Recent findings suggest that peach clafoutis is a traditional French dessert, with baked golden edges and a custardy center. A Sweet Thyme’s recipe includes a splash of bourbon and vanilla to deepen the peach flavor, but you’ll be surprised by how easy this showstopper is to make.

With Family Fresh Meals’ recipe, you don’t even have to turn on the oven. You’re literally just whipping together a handful of ingredients, smoothing it into a pie crust, and letting it set in the refrigerator. But nothing makes you feel more like the hostess with the mostest than whipping out a gorgeous pie at the end of dinner.

Sources indicate that ina Garten’s viral brownie pudding has a delicious crust with gooey, fudgy goodness underneath. Feel Good Foodie’s version simplifies the ingredient list, and it’s really just a matter of dumping things into a mixer before baking.

BRB while I become known as the strawberry-mascarpone-tart friend...

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

Industry observers note that labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

Robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a new product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

Kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she states. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

The claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, indicates Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

Sources indicate that the label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, notes Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

Industry observers note that kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she indicates. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

It has been revealed that protein and fiber make a massive difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she says. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

Industry observers note that most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, says Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

Sources indicate that hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

According to recent reports, seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she says, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”.

She’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she says.

Unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” notes Kaiden.

Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

To make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

It has been revealed that kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she says, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the fresh film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is at the moment the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”.

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Sources indicate that many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sources indicate that sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

Recent findings suggest that if you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

#56216. Baking My Nana's Recipes Reminds Me Of The Kind of Mom She Taught Me To Be

Baking My Nana's Recipes Reminds Me Of The Kind of Mom She Taught Me To Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.
  • Sources indicate that my Nana was not a good cook.
  • Her baking though, now that was good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The coziness of the holidays gets me all sentimental.

Sources indicate that my Nana was not a good cook. Not really. Her food was always basic. Good, but basic. I know this now that I am grown and trying to figure out if I’m a good cook myself. She was Irish and had about 12 things she knew how to cook and they were basically all holiday menu-specific. She could do up a roast turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy. A bag of coleslaw with a bottle of creamy dressing tossed in. She bought those little grocery store dinner rolls and popped them in the oven to warm as my Grandpa carved the turkey, his only chance to shine in the winter season as the barbeque was no longer an option.

Her baking though, now that was good. A bit better than good by ‘80s standards since the Great British Baking Show didn’t exist. She made excellent sticky buns and little donuts she shook in paper bags of cinnamon and sugar while they were piping hot. She baked birthday cakes for all of the grandchildren, chocolate and peanut butter, or strawberry cream, or white cake with jam in the middle.

Most of all, she baked raisin bread. Loaf after loaf of raisin bread for everyone she knew. We’ve never found the recipe in the two decades that she has been gone, and it is the thing her whole family misses the most. The dark, molasses smell of it. A nod to her Nova Scotian heritage. Sturdy enough to toast if you cut your morning slab extra thick. Sturdy enough for a great big smear of peanut butter too. A singular flavor I will miss forever.

Her raisin bread and cinnamon buns and chocolate cakes were not the things that drew us all to her kitchen. Her turkey wasn’t even really moist enough to have us all clamoring for late night sandwiches, and yet there we stood. Every year. Daughters and sons, grandchildren, friends. Some of us in pajamas, others in track pants to accommodate our food babies. My quiet Grandpa hovering around the periphery, hoping someone would make him a plate of food. We came for the sandwich but mostly we came for her. My Nana. A short, bossy, contrary matriarch who made messes, made toast with marmalade on cold mornings, made cup after cup of tea left too long on the stove.

According to recent reports, she made me want to be just like her. To call my loves back to my own kitchen. To make people feel welcome and loved and relaxed and just seen, all the time she was seeing us out of the corner of her eye. “What’s wrong?” she’d ask me as she was kneading cinnamon-scented dough for her raisin bread, all casual and relaxed as a viper ready to strike. She knew, she always knew, we came to her kitchen to pray at her feet. To talk out a breakup or a newly introduced love or a money problem over plates of eggs fried too hard, bread toasted too long. Almost always with a toddler sitting at her feet, a baby on her hip. A smile on her face.

It has been revealed that her technique in the kitchen was really more of a siren song. She chose her smells wisely, I think. She favoured cinnamon over chocolate. Rosemary over garlic. Warm hug smells. Luring us in for a gossip, her favorite appetizer for any meal. Did you hear? Guess who’s dating? You didn’t hear this from me… A buffet of talking and food, of mess and chaos.

Sources indicate that it has been 20 years since she died. I am as old as she was when I was a little girl, our golden hour together. And yet, she looms as large now in my holiday kitchen as she did when I was a girl.

Recent findings suggest that it is her voice I hear when I call out to my own sons, “Who’s hungry?” and make us all a big pot of chili to eat while we watch The Lord of the Rings for the hundredth time in the dark quiet of our living room. Or a great stack of buttermilk pancakes to be eaten with overly crisp bacon and real maple syrup, all of us sleepy at our table.

In a recent development, it was even her voice I heard in my oldest son when he told me he would like to take over Christmas morning breakfast. I sat in the kitchen, a cup of tea at my elbow, as he and his brothers made eggs benedict for all of us. One making artful pour over coffee, another seasoning hashbrowns, still another carefully poaching eggs and adding lemon to his homemade bechamel.

Sources indicate that the food has improved, but the heart of it stays the same. We come back to this kitchen that is not her kitchen but also is her kitchen.

Jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

#56214. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

📅 15 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1490 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

📅 15 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that pretend you’re a tree.
  • Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class.
  • Sources indicate that at the same time, I was physical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the major sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

Sources indicate that at the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Industry observers note that swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

Industry observers note that and what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

Recent findings suggest that no escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Sources indicate that like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more key, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one key lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

Apparently, part of adulting is developing a genuine appreciation for cooking. Who would’ve thought?

Now, I’m not saying I’m in my Julia Child era by any means. But I do dabble with scratch-made pasta sauce and homemade spicy beef noodles. That mentioned, when it comes to lazy nights at home or feeding a crowd, I’m never opposed to taking a few shortcuts... especially when they save me both time and money.

Recent findings suggest that as someone who exclusively grocery shops at Trader Joe’s, I’ve tried just about every side dish in the book. Whether you’re finalizing your Taco Tuesday menu or looking for a few last-minute additions to your holiday feast, TJ’s has plenty of options to please everyone at the table, even the picky little eaters. Better yet, some of these can pull double duty at both breakfast and dinner.

And to sweeten the deal, all these side dishes from Trader Joe’s make multiple servings for less than $6. Now that’s something worth adding to your cart.

Breakfast called, it wants an upgrade. This roasted potato, pepper, and onion medley brings a little room-service flair to your morning, with barely more effort than a few tosses in the pan. Serve it alongside steak and eggs, ideally over easy or poached — but it’s your breaky, your rules.

According to recent reports, (Tip: It also makes a pretty delicious dinner side with bratwurst or pork chops. Turns out, it’s got range.).

Looking for a dinner party side that would even wow the socks off Ina Garten? These kung pao Brussels sprouts are just the ticket. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go.
  • Industry observers note that in an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Waxing and waning signs, vague symptoms that come and go. A cat that is on deathâs door one moment, running around the next. Detecting illness in cats can be difficult enough, but when the body starts attacking itself, diagnosis becomes even more of a challenge.

Industry observers note that in an autoimmune disease, a catâs immune system malfunctions and begins attacking the body it is meant to protect. Fortunately, autoimmune disease is relatively uncommon in cats, but it can be serious and difficult to diagnose and treat. Because the signs tend to be vague and can come and go, they are easy to overlook, which makes it worth knowing what to watch for and when to involve a vet.

A healthy immune system protects the body from germs such as viruses and bacteria by sending out specialized cells to locate and destroy them. It also helps clear away damaged or diseased cells. These immune cells use protein signals on the surface of the bodyâs own cells to recognize them as safe. In autoimmune disease, a signaling error causes the immune system to treat the catâs own cells as a threat, and healthy, working tissue gets attacked and destroyed.

Cats can develop these problems much as people do. They can affect any part of the body, including the internal organs, blood, and skin, and there are many different types. Some can be life-threatening, weakening the bodyâs natural defenses while also damaging healthy tissue.

It has been revealed that the part of the body under attack determines which signs appear, so the picture varies dramatically from one cat to the next. Signs are often general and not immediately linked to an autoimmune problem. Possible signs include lethargy, weakness, decreased appetite, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and other changes to the feces. Other signs include pale gums, unexplained bleeding, bruising, a high temperature, a faster heart rate, rapid breathing, and tiring easily during play. Limping, swollen joints, sores on the skin, a poor coat, increased thirst, increased urination, and collapse are also on the list.

In a recent development, many of these signs come and go. A cat may seem completely fine one day and be struggling the next. Any of these signs are a reason to contact a vet promptly, since starting investigations early makes a real difference.

According to recent reports, the problem starts with the catâs own immune system, which is part of what makes it so hard to manage. The exact triggers are not fully understood, and more research is needed. An immune-mediated condition can be triggered when the immune system is stimulated. Viral infections, vaccination, medications, inherited conditions, and hormones have all been linked to autoimmune disease. Where things get tricky is that the incident that triggered the disease is not usually the cause of the disease. That means that the same type of autoimmune disease can be triggered by different things in different individuals.

Some of these conditions can be passed down, and other possible contributors include poor nutrition, toxins, cancer, and stress. A cat diagnosed with an autoimmune disease considered hereditary should not be bred under any circumstances.

Diagnosis is often a process of elimination. More common causes of the same signs are investigated and ruled out first, which can mean lots of tests. A vet will start with a full physical exam and a detailed history, then choose tests to fit the signs. These may include blood and urine tests, X-rays, or an ultrasound scan. Samples may also be taken from wounds, rashes, or other affected areas. Prompt diagnosis is key for effective management.

Treatment depends on the type of autoimmune disease, what part of the body is affected, and what is behind it, so it varies greatly. The usual approach is medication that calms the immune system so it stops attacking the body, most often corticosteroids like prednisone or dexamethasone. A large starting dose is often given, and once the signs settle down, the dose is lowered gradually.

According to recent reports, sometimes, stronger immunosuppressive drugs are also used. Some of them are also used in cancer treatment, and the side effects tend to be more severe. The trouble with treating an immune-mediated disease is that we are using medication to suppress the immune system, and that leaves the patient more susceptible to infection and other diseases.

Even more challenging when treating feline autoimmune disease is that some of the medications used to treat dogs or humans are toxic to cats.

Supportive care matters just as much. Pain relief is often needed, but many commonly prescribed anti-inflammatory painkillers cannot be given alongside steroids. Stronger painkillers like opioids or gabapentin may be used to manage severe pain, and these come with their own side effects. Antibiotics may also be prescribed, either prophylactically if extremely high doses of immunosuppressive medications are being used, or if secondary infections develop.

For cats with immune-mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA), where the immune system is attacking and destroying red blood cells, or immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP) where platelets are being destroyed, blood or plasma transfusions may be needed to save a catâs life.

Lifestyle changes can help too. A cat with painful, swollen joints, for example, benefits from losing weight if overweight, and lower sides on litter trays and softer beds make life more comfortable. Each case is assessed individually.

One of the more common autoimmune diseases in cats is known as Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex, a group of idiopathic conditions that are right now quite poorly understood. The exact cause of the disease is unknown; however, parasites, allergies, and genetic factors have been identified as likely triggers.

There are three main clinical presentations of eosinophilic granuloma complex:.

It has been revealed that ulcerative: Also known as indolent ulcers or rodent ulcers, this form of eosinophilic granuloma complex usually presents with a sore on the cat's mouth. It is typically seen on the upper lip. They are normally red in color and do not appear to cause your cat any pain or irritation.

Plaque-forming: often found on the stomach and on the inside of the hind legs. The lesions are often itchy and red and often become infected, which complicates matters.

Granuloma forming: usually presents as raised pink or yellow nodules that can be located anywhere on your cat.

Industry observers note that another more common feline immune-mediated disease is called pemphigus foliaceus. It affects the skin, causing scabs, crusts, and sores around the eyes and ears, on the paws, and in the groin area. When it develops on the paws, the nail beds can be affected as well.

According to recent reports, there is no cure for autoimmune disease, but effective treatment and management can control the signs, greatly improve quality of life, and allow most cats to live fairly comfortably. These conditions can be debilitating and life-threatening, yet it is often possible to manage them well enough for cats to lead relatively normal lives. Because the signs overlap with so many other conditions, a vet visit at the first sign that something is wrong is the surest way to get answers early.

10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.
  • Recent findings suggest that finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough.
  • Sources indicate that sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Recent findings suggest that finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sources indicate that sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

In a recent development, the 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Recent findings suggest that who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Industry observers note that everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

In a recent development, not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Sources indicate that here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

Sources indicate that one of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

According to recent reports, not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

Industry observers note that you can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

It has been revealed that the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

Industry observers note that each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide. The list is built from a full year of Search trends across every category from tech to style. And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list claims about how we’re shopping this year.

Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

It has been revealed that “A ton of play,” Google wrote, and we respect the pun. Searches for stuffed elephant plushies rose 240%, with the Pets Alive Baby Elephant Surprise as the featured pick. Plush is a good pick for a 1-year-old and a 10-year-old alike, and the right one becomes a friend for life.

Searches for the Fujifilm instax holiday set jumped 190%. For tweens, a camera that spits out a real photo is a nice break from the phone, and the prints end up taped to bedroom walls instead of buried in a camera roll. They’ll fly through the film, so tuck a couple of extra packs in the box.

Recent findings suggest that searches for the FAO Schwarz Piano Mat “struck a chord,” rising 180% in 2026. Anyone who watched Tom Hanks stomp out a duet on the giant keyboard in “Big” wanted one of these, and the floor-sized version now fits in a playroom. It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

Searches for “adjustable roller skates” cruised up 180%. Adjustable skates expand across several sizes, so they can outlast a growth spurt or two. Just remember to add a helmet and pads to the cart.

Some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a massive share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

It has been revealed that late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

It has been revealed that the back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

Recent findings suggest that these are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

It has been revealed that I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

Industry observers note that the subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

I don’t do major speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

According to recent reports, it’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

In a recent development, I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

It has been revealed that every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A latest school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

Sources indicate that I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

Recent findings suggest that so on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been mentioned when the moment comes.

In a recent development, back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

That’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more important ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Recent findings suggest that teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

Industry observers note that I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

It has been revealed that I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

Sources indicate that we spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

Drinks You Can Make By The Batch

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater.
  • These punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-strategy prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16.
  • Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bring something good. Let the grown-ups serve themselves.

Industry observers note that holiday magic is a lot of unpaid labor in an ugly Christmas sweater. Between class potlucks, Thanksgiving logistics and buying the only bread your kid will eat, you’ve got enough on your plate. Now add holiday parties, questionable white elephant gifts and 400 things to do before the doorbell rings. The last thing you need is a second job as a bartender.

These punches, pitchers and alcohol-free drinks are perfect for pre-strategy prepping.There’s a spicy margarita you can carry in the tequila bottle, a pear punch for the fancy friends, and a peppermint espresso martini you can make for 16. Some need a little attention before serving. Most are ready to pour once chilled.

Julie Reiner, co-founder of Brooklyn’s Clover Club, served punch and freezer cocktails at a Halloween party for 20. “The goal is to spend time with your guests, not be stuck behind the bar all night!” she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that A little planning helps. Julianna McIntosh, the cocktail creator behind Join Jules, recommends using fresh citrus the day of your party and accounting for the water normally added when you shake or stir a drink with ice. Hannah Chamberlain, the recipe developer behind Spirited LA, has another rule: Hold the ice and bubbly until guests arrive. Otherwise, you risk a watered-down punch with flat bubbles.

It has been revealed that bringing a batch to someone else’s party? Pack it in a tightly sealed container, keep it chilled and add the bubbles when you arrive. Then pour yourself a glass and let someone else worry about the rest.

It has been revealed that bitter, bubbly and ridiculously easy to scale up. Natalie Migliarini, the cocktail creator behind Beautiful Booze, makes her Negroni Sbagliato with equal parts Select Aperitivo, sweet vermouth and prosecco, finished with an orange slice. The recipe makes one, but you can multiply the aperitivo and vermouth to serve your group, then chill them together in a bottle. When it's time to drink, pour over ice, add the prosecco and stir. No shaker required.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

According to recent reports, everyone’s due at six. The first guest rings the bell at 5:42. Have Reiner’s Boat House Punch ready. Gin, Aperol, St-Germain and three citrus juices get a bright, bittersweet lift from sparkling rosé. “I always want my punch to be a crowd-pleaser, but it needs to have a little personality too!” Reiner remarked. This makes a substantial batch, so save it for a crowd. Let the lemon peels and sugar sit for at least an hour or overnight, and freeze a large ice block ahead of time. Add the ice and rosé just before serving.

Get the recipe at Cocktails Distilled.

Industry observers note that champagne tastes even better when nobody has to mix 12 individual cocktails. Chamberlain's large-batch take on the French 75 combines gin, fresh lemon, orange bitters and homemade cranberry-ginger syrup, then gets topped with sparkling wine. It serves six to eight and looks impressive without requiring an elaborate garnish situation. Make the syrup ahead and chill the ingredients. When guests arrive, add large ice cubes and the bubbly, give it a stir, and you're done. If the finished punch tastes a little dull, Chamberlain recommends adding a few dashes of Angostura or cardamom bitters to give it more personality.

Industry observers note that love your friends. Not enough to muddle each of them a mojito. Averie Sunshine’s pomegranate mojito punch at Averie Cooks combines white rum, mint, pomegranate juice and seeds, lemon and sparkling water in one pitcher. It makes four generous drinks, so double it for a bigger gathering. Chill the liquids ahead, then muddle the mint and assemble the punch just before serving so the leaves stay fresh, and the bubbles don't disappear. Ice goes in the glasses. One round of muddling. Everybody gets a drink.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

According to recent reports, here, Chamberlain pairs pear nectar with gin, ginger liqueur, rosemary syrup, lemon, cardamom bitters and dry bubbly in her Calling Card Punch. It's an elegant, herbal alternative to the usual holiday punch and serves six to eight. Make the rosemary syrup ahead, chill the ingredients and add the sparkling wine while serving.

“I tend to build my punch a little less sweet and then I’ll often have a little extra syrup I can add if it seems unbalanced,” Chamberlain said. It's easier to add sweetness than take it away.

By the time dessert rolls around, the adults deserve something stronger than another cup of coffee. McIntosh combines vodka, espresso or cold brew, coffee liqueur and peppermint syrup for a holiday spin on the espresso martini. Her large-batch version makes about 16 servings, with no individual shaking required. Mix everything ahead, chill it in the freezer for about two hours and give it a quick whirl in the blender if you want that signature foam. Pour into a punch bowl and let everyone help themselves. Crushed candy cane rims are optional. You've already done enough decorating.

Give the alcohol-free drinks their own spot at the party. America’s Test Kitchen combines cranberries, ginger, rosemary, cinnamon and star anise in a sweetened base you can make up to four days ahead. When guests arrive, add chilled cranberry juice, orange juice and seltzer. It makes 16 servings, enough for an open house where another family keeps appearing in the doorway.

Get the recipe at America’s Test Kitchen.

The tiny apple leaves are optional – you have enough crafts coming home from school. Chamberlain’s Fallen Leaves Punch mixes cognac, tart apple cider and lemon with homemade cranberry-cinnamon syrup for eight servings. It's a good Friendsgiving option if you want something tart, fruity and a little stronger than cider.

“In terms of flavor combinations, it’s hard to disappoint with the combination of seasonal spice and fruit,” Chamberlain remarked. Make the syrup ahead, squeeze the lemons the day of and stir everything over a large ice block at serving.

Taco night doesn’t need a November makeover. McIntosh makes six spicy margaritas right in the tequila bottle, giving you a batch and a carrying container in one. You'll need to pour out some tequila first; the recipe tells you how much. Mix everything in the bottle, then let it sit in the freezer for 2 to 4 hours, then pour it over ice into salt-rimmed glasses. All the fun of margaritas without anyone spending the evening squeezing limes.

Apple cider is doing a lot of heavy lifting this holiday season, let it have some rum. Chamberlain's Cider Rum Punch combines tart cider, aged pineapple rum, lemon, orange bitters and a homemade mulling-spice syrup for six servings. She makes it every year, and it's easy to see why. The warm spices play nicely with the fruit without turning the whole thing into a scented candle. Make the syrup ahead, then combine everything in a pitcher with plenty of ice and stir until chilled. Bonus: There's no sparkling wine to worry about going flat.

It has been revealed that the kids’ table and Grandma can drink from the same pitcher. McIntosh’s pineapple passion fruit agua fresca blends tropical fruit, lime and agave into six refreshing alcohol-free servings. Frozen passion fruit pulp works, and there are no bubbles to go flat on the drive. Make it up to two days ahead, refrigerate and give it a good stir before pouring over ice.

According to recent reports, after the holiday lights walk, everyone comes home freezing and suddenly needs something warm RIGHT NOW. Sunshine's peppermint white hot chocolate at Averie Cooks combines milk, melted white chocolate and a little peppermint extract. The recipe makes five mugs, but you can easily double or triple it for a houseful of cold kids and grown-ups. Heat everything together over low heat, stirring until the chocolate melts. Don't let it boil, and go easy on the peppermint. A little goes a long way. Add marshmallows if you've got them. Nobody's going to complain.

Get the recipe at Averie Cooks.

Recent findings suggest that the wine people and the margarita people can share a pitcher. Migliarini’s tequila sangria at Beautiful Booze combines Sauvignon Blanc with tequila, cranberry syrup, fresh cranberries, red and green apples and lime. “Keeping it simple, my recipe includes fruits that are available throughout the entire year,” she writes in the recipe. It serves five to six, making it a good choice for a casual Friendsgiving. Chill the wine, tequila and fruit mixture ahead, then add the lemon-lime soda just before serving.

Get the recipe at Beautiful Booze.

No fish. Promise. Amy Traynor’s Fish House Punch at Moody Mixologist combines cognac and aged rum with peach liqueur, lemon and cold black tea. Think peach iced tea with considerably more going on. Her recipe includes a version for 10, so there's no need to multiply or do any guesswork. Freeze a large ice block ahead, stir the ingredients over it at serving and finish each glass with freshly grated nutmeg. Fair warning: This one's boozy.

Get the recipe at Moody Mixologist.

Dinner’s over, the kids have claimed the television and nobody’s ready to leave. Put a pot of McIntosh’s mulled Aperol on the stove for the spritz drinkers still on your sofa. Dry white wine, Aperol, apple cider and honey warm with orange and whole spices. It makes six servings and needs just 15 to 20 minutes over low heat. Don't let it boil. Ladle into mugs and let everyone settle in. The kitchen will smell like you had a initiative.
